Edition note: An independent English rewriting for English-language readers, preserving the Chinese argument while reorganizing context, sequence, and emphasis. Full-series spoilers.

Fifty-Four Million

Soon after becoming mayor, Tommy Carcetti learns that Baltimore's school system has a fifty-four-million-dollar deficit. The number destroys the plans on which he campaigned: police raises, a unit that investigates real crimes, and an end to juked statistics. The school gap must be filled, and the money has to come from somewhere.

His staff proposes asking Annapolis for help. The Republican governor has the funds, but Carcetti is a Democrat preparing to run against him for governor in two years. After making Carcetti wait, the governor offers the bailout on two conditions: the state will receive partial control of the schools, and Carcetti will stand beside him at a press conference while the governor announces that he has rescued Baltimore's children from the city's mismanagement. The images will later become campaign advertising.

Carcetti refuses. Norman Wilson, his adviser and one of the show's least accommodating truth-tellers, makes his disapproval plain.

His explanation is not a simple lie. Taking the money would damage his statewide campaign; losing that campaign would prevent him from exercising greater power; with greater power, he believes he could do more for Baltimore. He exchanges a certain loss in the present—the schools' immediate need—for a possible benefit in the future.

That calculation requires one hidden constant: Carcetti must remain the person occupying the next position. The children bearing this year's cuts become the discounted cost of his future usefulness. From then on, “I need to stay on the path to greater power so I can eventually do greater good” can explain nearly every choice he makes.

Each Decision Makes Sense Alone

The Wire does not turn Carcetti into a secret fraud. It does something more unsettling. It lets a decent and capable man travel toward conduct he once despised without supplying a single moment at which he plainly becomes corrupt.

He limits Commissioner Burrell because Burrell manipulates statistics. That is defensible. He promotes Cedric Daniels because Daniels wants cases rather than numbers. Also defensible. He reduces the severity of a brutality complaint against Herc after Daniels argues that discipline should be proportionate and the department is already unstable. There is a reason. He cuts police raises because the school deficit is arithmetic. He refuses state money because, within his long-term account, a gubernatorial victory matters more.

Eventually he needs favorable crime numbers for that campaign. The demand he once condemned returns under his own administration. When the polished reports arrive, he knows how they were made. He does not order anyone to falsify them. He simply stops asking.

That is what metric distortion looks like at the top. The person receiving the number need not alter a single report. He only has to accept the answer while declining to inspect the method.

Every step grows from the pressure created by the previous step, and the first step was sincere. Moral decline here does not look like one large betrayal. It looks like a sequence of individually articulate reasons.

The Person Changes; the Position Remains

Clarence Royce, Carcetti's predecessor, jukes crime statistics, protects loyal subordinates, and thinks constantly about reelection. The series does not present him as a monster. He is a man who has occupied the office long enough to know its demands. He even considers keeping Hamsterdam when it appears to work, then withdraws the thought when its political cost becomes clear.

Carcetti wins by attacking Royce. Within two years he is performing the same operations.

This is the show's most direct account of an institution. It is not merely a building, a rulebook, or a collection of bad personalities. It is a set of positions. The mayoral position asks its occupant to protect a budget, prepare for the next election, display results before the campaign begins, and preserve the coalition that put him there. It asks these things of Royce and Carcetti in the same language.

The person changes; the position remains. And the position is often harder than the person. The final essay will follow that pattern through the closing montage, beyond the mayor to police, reporters, corner workers, and people living with addiction.

That does not make personal choice meaningless. It makes the object of choice clearer. A person in office is not deciding only between policies. He is repeatedly deciding whether preserving the office—and his own continued presence within it—will count as part of the public good.

The Middle

Cedric Daniels is perhaps the series' strongest example of a good person trying to remain inside. He is competent, principled, protective of his people, and openly committed to real investigations. Carcetti raises him for exactly those reasons. When Daniels finally reaches the commissioner's office, he is asked to deliver the homicide numbers political leadership needs. He refuses. An unresolved financial irregularity from his early career, held in reserve for years, is used to force him out. The position passes to someone who will comply.

Ellis Carver begins at the opposite end. In the first season he treats policing as arrests, force, and fun. Colvin tells him that he does not know the people in his own district and therefore is not really policing it; he is merely collecting statistics. Carver changes. He learns names, stays in his sector, attends to children, and tries desperately to protect Randy.

He cannot protect him. At the end of the series Carver is promoted into the office Daniels once occupied. The show offers no judgment, only the visual rhyme. Daniels also began lower in the hierarchy. Carver's growth is genuine, and the office's demands are genuine. The unanswered question is what will happen when the two meet.

Institutions live through this middle level. People there can translate pressure downward, resist it temporarily, or bear its cost themselves. They can also be removed and replaced. The more a structure depends on exceptional individuals to keep it humane, the more fragile its humanity remains.

Looking Out the Window

After his election, Carcetti briefly encounters the bodily reality beneath the reports and admits to Norman Wilson that he sometimes forgets what the numbers contain. Norman's advice is simple: go look more often.

Carcetti does not. A mayor faces a hundred urgent matters, each with a meeting and a deadline. Going to see what the number means has no deadline. The things capable of summoning him always defeat the thing that cannot summon him.

This may be the most practical observation in the chapter. A position need not transform someone's beliefs overnight. It only has to arrange attention. What can demand an immediate response moves forward; what cannot waits. “Who is living under this statistic?” almost never sends a calendar invitation.

We often ask whether a public figure has forgotten his original purpose. Carcetti probably remembers it. Memory is not the problem. He can give a coherent reason for each departure, and each reason preserves an image of the future in which his rise will make the departures worthwhile.

Think of something your current position asks you to accept that you would have rejected two years ago. The important question is not whether you can justify it. You probably can. The question is whether the reason is yours—or whether the position prepared it for you.

Next we return to the middle school. An unsuccessful police officer becomes a teacher; a district commander driven out of the force becomes a research assistant. Each discovers something that works. Both efforts are stopped, although nobody opposes the good they accomplish. Essay V: The School.

The Wire, created by David Simon, aired from 2002 to 2008 across five seasons and sixty episodes. This essay relies on the series itself.
